title: The Science of Birds
author: Ivan Phillipsen
description: A lighthearted exploration of bird biology, hosted by a professional birding guide with a PhD in Zoology. Learn about the fascinating world of birds and pick up some ornithology facts along the way.

episodes.title: Random Bird Thursday: A Highly Vocal Species With Female Helpers
episodes.summary: Ivan profiles the White-throated Magpie-Jay, a loud Central American bird with an unusual cooperative breeding system in which female helpers assist in raising the young.

episodes.title: Grebes
episodes.summary: Episode 137 dives into the family Podicipedidae: the lobed toes and rear-set legs, the synchronized courtship dances, the surprising identity of grebes' closest relatives, why they swallow their own feathers, and how they raise chicks on floating nests.

episodes.title: Random Bird Thursday: A Citrus-themed Species with Runny Mascara
episodes.summary: A short spotlight on the Orange-headed Thrush, an Asian songbird with striking facial markings and colorful plumage.

episodes.title: From the Field: Australia
episodes.summary: Ivan shares stories from guiding a birding trip across Australia, from Outback deserts to tropical rainforest, and previews a future expedition.

episodes.title: Random Bird Thursday: A Duet-singer That Uses Bones for Decoration
episodes.summary: The Rufous Cacholote, a South American ovenbird known for singing duets and decorating its nest with bones.

episodes.title: Random Bird Thursday: A Tiny Island Dweller That Likes Vines
episodes.summary: The Rufous-sided Gerygone, a tiny island songbird with specialized foraging habits among vines.

articles.question: Is a grebe a duck?
articles.metaDescription: No. Grebes aren't ducks, loons or coots. Ivan Phillipsen of The Science of Birds explains their lobed toes, feather-eating and wild courtship dances.
articles.intro: No. A grebe is not a duck, even though it swims like one and gets mistaken for one constantly. In episode 137 of The Science of Birds, host Ivan Phillipsen, a zoologist and birding guide, explains that grebes belong to their own family, Podicipedidae, and that their closest living relatives are a group of birds nobody would guess. Once you know what to look for, you'll never confuse a grebe with a duck again.

sections.heading: Ducks have webbed feet. Grebes have something weirder.
sections.body:
The fastest way to tell a grebe from a duck is to look at the feet, if you ever get the chance. Ducks have the classic webbed foot, with skin stretched between the toes like a paddle. Grebes don't. Instead, each toe carries its own separate flap of skin, so the foot looks like a set of leaves. Ivan describes these as lobed toes, and they work brilliantly for a bird that spends its life diving.

The legs are also set far back on the body, right near the tail. That's perfect for propulsion underwater, where grebes chase fish and invertebrates, but terrible for walking. On land a grebe can barely shuffle, which is why you almost never see one out of the water. The show notes link to a video of a Western Grebe walking on a beach, and it looks about as graceful as you'd expect.

The bill is another giveaway. Ducks have broad, flattened bills for dabbling and straining. Grebes have pointed, dagger-like bills for grabbing prey. Put those together, pointed bill, no visible tail, sitting low in the water and vanishing under the surface for long stretches, and you're looking at a grebe.

sections.heading: Their closest cousins are flamingos
sections.body:
Here's the part of the episode that surprises everyone. For a long time ornithologists assumed grebes were related to loons, since both are diving birds with similar body plans. Genetic studies turned that idea upside down. Grebes' closest living relatives are flamingos.

Ivan explains that the resemblance between grebes and loons is a case of convergent evolution: two unrelated lineages arrived at the same shape because they solve the same problem, catching food underwater. The grebe-flamingo connection is supported by DNA and by some subtle shared anatomical features, and the two groups are now placed together in a clade called Mirandornithes.

So the bird bobbing on your local pond is, in evolutionary terms, more closely related to a pink wading bird from a salt lagoon than to the ducks it's swimming with.

sections.heading: Why grebes swallow their own feathers
sections.body:
One of the strangest habits in the bird world gets a full explanation in this episode. Grebes eat their own feathers, in large quantities, and they feed feathers to their chicks too.

The leading explanation is that the feathers form a soft plug in the stomach. Grebes eat fish with sharp bones and hard-shelled invertebrates, and a mat of feathers may protect the stomach lining and slow the passage of indigestible bits until they can be broken down or coughed up as a pellet. The host walks through the evidence and notes that while the exact function is still debated, the behavior is universal across the family, which suggests it matters.

It's a good reminder that a lot of what looks bizarre in animals is a solution to a problem we just haven't thought about.

sections.heading: Dances on water and nests that float
sections.body:
If you've seen a viral clip of two birds sprinting side by side across the surface of a lake, you've seen grebes. That's the rushing ceremony of Western and Clark's Grebes, one of the most spectacular courtship displays of any bird. Pairs also perform a weed ceremony, rising chest to chest out of the water while holding bits of aquatic vegetation. Great Crested Grebes in Europe do a similar dance, and the show notes link to videos of all of them.

Ivan explains that these highly synchronized displays help pairs form and maintain bonds, and both sexes participate equally.

After all that, grebes build a floating nest of rotting vegetation anchored to reeds. It's a soggy, precarious platform, and the eggs sit partly in water. Once the chicks hatch, they climb onto a parent's back and ride there, tucked under the wings, while the adult swims and even dives. If you ever see a grebe with a striped fuzzy head poking out of its feathers, that's a chick hitching a ride.

keyTakeaways: Grebes are their own family, Podicipedidae, not ducks, loons or coots.
Look for lobed toes instead of webbed feet, a pointed bill, legs set far back, and a bird that dives rather than dabbles.
DNA shows grebes' closest relatives are flamingos. Their resemblance to loons is convergent evolution.
Grebes swallow their own feathers, probably to cushion the stomach against fish bones and other sharp prey.
Their synchronized courtship dances are among the most dramatic in the bird world, and chicks ride on the parents' backs.

faq.q: How do I tell a grebe from a coot or a loon?
faq.a: Coots have a white chicken-like bill and bob their heads as they swim. Loons are much larger with heavy bills and a checkered back in summer. Grebes are small to medium, sit low, have thin pointed bills and almost no visible tail.
Most species can, and many migrate long distances, but they need a running takeoff across the water and rarely fly except when traveling. A few island species have lost the ability to fly entirely.

faq.q: Why do grebes carry their chicks on their backs?
faq.a: The nest is a wet floating platform, so chicks leave it soon after hatching. Riding on a parent's back keeps them warm and safe from predators while the adults swim and forage.
